parsed.attack: The behaviour this depends on - a seventeen-year-old voluntarily authoring careful line-level analysis for classmates in their exam year - is the opposite of what exam-year students actually do, which is hunt for someone else's notes: PMT, Seneca, SparkNotes and shared Quizlet sets are all consumption, and in a graded cohort competing for the same university places the incentive to publish your best reading of a line is negative. The author already knows this: a kill threshold of three student-written annotations per set text per class per full term is an extraordinarily low bar, and setting it that low is an admission that authorship is expected to be near zero. Where the arguing does happen it happens free in the class WhatsApp group and a shared Google Doc, with no onboarding and no link to distribute. Finally the money does not exist - students do not hold payment methods and will not subscribe, parents buy tutors not annotation tools, and schools procure through channels the wedge does not touch.
parsed.strongest_defence: Twenty percent adding one note is the realistic ask, not mass authorship - a class needs two or three vocal students to seed it and everyone else gets value reading - and the pre-mock resurfacing of the highest-rated line notes is the moment that converts, with the teacher, not the student, as the real distributor and the school as the eventual payer.
parsed.verdict_reason: It depends on teenage authorship and teenage payment, both behaviours the evidence runs against, though a small seeding cohort plus teacher-led distribution is a coherent escape.
